scenes.text: In the early hours of September 1992, London was quiet, but Britain's financial system was already moving toward a historic confrontation.
At the center of the coming crisis stood the Bank of England, responsible for defending the value of the British pound.
Britain was tied to continental Europe through a monetary arrangement designed to keep major European currencies relatively stable.
For sterling, that promise would soon become extremely difficult to keep.
The system was known as the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, or ERM.
Inside the ERM, currencies were expected to remain within agreed exchange-rate bands.
Sterling could move, but only within a limited range before the authorities were expected to intervene.
Maintaining that range meant interest rates could not simply be set according to Britain's domestic needs.
That was a serious problem, because the British economy was already struggling.
Recession had weakened businesses, households, and confidence across the country.
At the same time, inflation remained an important concern for policymakers.
Across Europe, another currency was exerting enormous influence: the German Deutsche Mark.
Germany's Bundesbank had become one of the most powerful central banks in Europe.
After German reunification, inflationary pressure encouraged the Bundesbank to maintain relatively high interest rates.
Britain now faced a dangerous mismatch between a weak domestic economy and tight European monetary conditions.
The pound was being pulled in two directions at once.
Lower rates could support Britain's economy, but they could also make sterling harder to defend.
Foreign-exchange traders began to recognize this contradiction.
Across dealing rooms, banks and funds watched sterling more closely.
Selling pressure against the pound gradually intensified.
Britain's government remained committed to defending the exchange rate.
To do that, the authorities could use Britain's foreign-exchange reserves.
The Bank of England could enter the market and buy pounds in an attempt to support sterling.
But intervention could only work if markets believed the policy was sustainable.
That belief was beginning to weaken.
Britain had fewer and fewer comfortable options.
Financial newspapers and trading desks increasingly discussed the possibility of a major currency crisis.
Markets watched every movement in sterling for signs that the defense was failing.
By September 1992, pressure around the pound was becoming increasingly difficult to contain.
The system had not yet broken, but the storm that would become Black Wednesday was now very close.
